guide.name: Sankofa
guide.welcome: Hi! I'm Sankofa. My name comes from an Akan symbol meaning "go back and fetch what was left behind". I know the machines NASA left in space. Pick a destination and I'll take you there.
guide.chooseBody: Click a world, or pick it from the list. Each one hosts a machine with a story to tell.

guide.noMachine: I don't have a story for {{body}} yet. Try another world!
guide.ready: Good choice. Back to Earth: that's where it all begins. Buckle up!
guide.handover: I'll leave you with {{machine}}. It will tell you its mission, from launch to the very end.
guide.outro: That's the end of {{machine}}'s story. Want to discover another machine?

body.name: The body
body.does: It protects the computer, batteries and electronics from the extreme cold.
body.why: Without it, the instruments would not survive the freezing nights.

wheels.name: The wheels
wheels.does: They let the machine move across ground covered in rocks and sand. On the big Mars rovers, a jointed "rocker-bogie" suspension keeps all six wheels on the ground.
wheels.why: The farther it drives, the more kinds of terrain it can study.

arm.name: The robotic arm
arm.does: It brings the instruments close to rocks to scratch, dig or analyse them.
arm.why: It is the robot's hand: without it, studying the ground up close would be impossible.

mast.name: The mast and its cameras
mast.does: It holds the cameras up high, like a head with eyes.
mast.why: The pictures are used to choose where to go and to study the landscape.

panels.name: The solar panels
panels.why: When dust covers them, power drops: that is what ended several missions.

legs.name: The landing legs
legs.does: They absorb the landing and keep the craft steady on the ground.
legs.why: One failed landing, and the whole mission is lost.

rotor.name: The blades
rotor.does: They spin very fast to push air down and lift the craft.
rotor.why: On Mars, the air is so thin that they must spin at more than 2,400 revolutions per minute.

antenna.name: The antenna
antenna.does: It sends data to Earth and receives the engineers' commands.
antenna.why: Without it, the machine could never tell what it discovered.

mirror.name: The mirrors
mirror.does: Glass "corner cubes" send light back exactly where it came from.
mirror.why: They let us measure the Earth–Moon distance to within a few millimetres.

engine.name: The descent engine
engine.does: It pushes downward to slow the descent.
engine.why: It is what made a soft landing possible.

power.name: The nuclear generator (RTG)
power.does: It makes electricity from the heat of a radioactive material.
power.why: It works day and night, even far from the Sun or under dust.

footpad.name: The footpads
footpad.does: These wide feet spread the craft's weight over the dust.
footpad.why: Before the first landings, nobody knew whether the lunar ground would be firm enough to hold a spacecraft.

ladder.name: The ladder
ladder.does: It links the module to the ground. Neil Armstrong climbed down it in July 1969 to take the first step on the Moon.
ladder.why: It is the passage between the spacecraft and the surface: the start of human exploration of the Moon.

seismometer.name: The seismometer
seismometer.does: It records ground vibrations: meteorite impacts, moonquakes.
seismometer.why: Waves travelling through the Moon reveal what lies inside, like an ultrasound scan.
